headline.statement: Results and Discussion report whole-cohort wound-complication rates of 12%, 10%, 18% and 20% by reprinting Table 1’s event counts as percentages of the same 397 women, whose table rates are 3%, 2.5%, 4.5% and 5%.
headline.evidence: Table 1: “Yes 12(3)”, “Yes 10(2.5)”, “Yes 18(4.5)”, “Yes 20(5)” of “n=397”. Results: “wound gapping occurred in 12% of cases, wound seroma occurred in 10% of cases, wound erythema occurred in 18% of cases, and wound infection occurred in 20% of cases in the whole cohort of cases.” Discussion repeats the same four percentages.
headline.plain: The authors wrote that 12, 10, 18 and 20 percent of all women had each wound problem, but their own table shows those were the numbers of women, not the percentages — the table rates are about 3, 2.5, 4.5 and 5 percent.

findings.title: Results and Discussion reprint Table 1 event counts as whole-cohort percentages
findings.location: Results Description and Discussion, whole-cohort wound-complication rates vs Table 1
findings.reported: Results: “wound gapping occurred in 12% of cases, wound seroma occurred in 10% of cases, wound erythema occurred in 18% of cases, and wound infection occurred in 20% of cases in the whole cohort of cases.” Discussion repeats “the percentage of wound gapping occurred in 12% of cases … wound infection occurred in 20% of cases.” Table 1, n=397: gapping 12 (3), seroma 10 (2.5), erythema 18 (4.5), infection 20 (5).
findings.computed: 12/397 = 3.02%, which matches Table 1’s printed 3% and not the prose 12% (implied denominator about 100, not 397). 10/397 = 2.52% vs prose 10%; 20/397 = 5.04% vs prose 20%. Stage 1: 18/397 prints as 4.5%. The Abstract reports the Table 4 p-values and odds ratios, not these inflated percentages.
findings.assumptions: The Results sentence states the rates are of the whole cohort; Table 1 gives n=397 after exclusion of 3 cases. The implied base of 100 is not a sample size the paper prints, which rules out a silent subgroup denominator. A 0-decimal 12% is attainable at n=397 as some other count, so this is a contradiction between two printed renderings of the same four numerators, not a granularity impossibility. Likeliest innocent reading: the event counts were pasted into a percentage sentence twice.
findings.plain: In two narrative sections the authors say 12, 10, 18 and 20 percent of the whole group had each wound problem. Their own table uses those same four numbers as head-counts, and the true shares of the 397 women are about four times smaller. A reader of the story will overstate how common the complications were; the head-to-head comparison between suture methods is a separate set of figures and is not changed by this.

passages.quote: wound gapping occurred in 12% of cases, wound seroma occurred in 10% of cases, wound erythema occurred in 18% of cases, and wound infection occurred in 20% of cases in the whole cohort of cases.
passages.label: Results, Description

consequence.explanation: The four whole-cohort complication rates in Results and Discussion are fourfold higher than Table 1; the interrupted-versus-continuous tests in Table 4 are unchanged.

findings.title: Table 2 BMI range starts at 23.0 while Methods excludes BMI below 30
findings.location: Table 2, BMI row vs Patients and methods inclusion criteria
findings.reported: Methods: “with BMI>30 (so, we do not have a group of women with BMI below 30 as our focus in the present research was to assess the obese women)”; exclusions include “women with BMI<30”. Table 2: “BMI 23.0–45.0 34.5±3.6 34.0”.
findings.computed: A contiguous Methods span that the sample contains no woman with BMI below 30 cannot both be true with a printed BMI minimum of 23.0. Mean 34.5 and median 34.0 remain compatible with an obese sample.
findings.assumptions: none beyond the paper's own statements. Innocent readings include a mistyped lower bound (33.0 printed as 23.0) or unreported protocol deviations. Stage 1 confirmed the 23.0–45.0 range on the PDF page image.
findings.plain: The methods say every woman had a body-mass index above 30 — that is the paper’s own rule for who was obese and who was enrolled — yet the summary table lists a lowest value of 23. Those two statements cannot both be right. The average and midpoint still look like an obese group, so a mistyped 23 for 33 is a live possibility, but the printed range as it stands includes women the authors said they did not have.

passages.quote: with BMI>30 (so, we do not have a group of women with BMI below 30 as our focus in the present research was to assess the obese women)
passages.label: Patients and methods, inclusion

consequence.explanation: The claim that the analysed cohort is obese women with BMI>30 is incompatible with the printed BMI range starting at 23.0.

findings.title: Table 3 subcutaneous-depth p=.127 does not match a t-test on the printed means
findings.computed: Welch two-tailed p = 0.295708 (t = 1.0471, df = 390.28); Student two-tailed p = 0.295573 (t = 1.0474, df = 395); one-tailed p = 0.147854. None matches reported p = 0.127 (p_matches false; difference 0.169). Both the printed and the recalculated values are above .05.
findings.assumptions: Group sizes n=198 and n=199 are taken from Table 4 column headers and Methods, not printed on Table 3 itself. The paper never names the test; Table 3 presents mean±SD with a p, and the other six Table 3 rows match independent t-tests, which is why a t-test is the working reading. A rank-sum test is not named and is not ruled out.
findings.plain: For thickness of the fat layer under the skin, the paper prints group averages 4.5 versus 4.4 centimetres and a probability of .127 that such a difference arose by chance. Recalculating from those averages and spreads gives a probability of about .30, not .127. Both figures still count as “not a statistically significant difference,” so the claim that the two suture groups started similar on this measure is unchanged. The paper never says which test produced .127.

consequence.explanation: Both the printed p=.127 and the recalculated p≈.296 are non-significant; the baseline “no difference” claim is unchanged.

report_markdown:
This trial randomised 400 women having a first caesarean to continuous or interrupted Vicryl 3-0 closure of the subcutaneous layer (analysed 198 vs 199) and concluded that interrupted closure is superior on four wound complications.

The arm-level comparisons that carry that conclusion check. Table 4’s four 2×2 tables reproduce the printed p-values and odds ratios (gapping 10/198 vs 2/199, p=.019, OR=5.239; seroma 9 vs 1, p=.011, OR=9.429; erythema 14 vs 4, p=.015, OR=3.709; infection 17 vs 3, p=.001, OR=6.136). Table 1’s n(%) cells, the composite 33+9=42 in Table 5, the flow-diagram cascade 411−11=400 with 200−1=199 and 200−2=198, six of seven Table 3 t-tests, the Table 6 odds-ratio intervals, and the suture-count reconstruction all reconcile. Forty-one of fifty checks passed; every granularity item matched on its printed values, with no rounding or population-SD allowance needed. Baseline similarity was unremarkable (similarity p=.883; τ̂=0.72).

What does not settle is how the same four event counts are written in prose. Table 1 prints 12 (3), 10 (2.5), 18 (4.5) and 20 (5) of 397. The Results description, and again the opening of the Discussion, call those 12%, 10%, 18% and 20% “of cases in the whole cohort.” That sentence names the 397-woman cohort as the base, so a silent subgroup denominator is not available as an explanation: 12 events in 397 is 3%, and the printed 12% implies a base of about 100, a size the paper never uses. The Abstract does not repeat the inflated rates. The likeliest innocent reading is that the numerators were pasted into a percentage sentence and never converted. A reader who uses the Discussion’s rates will think complications were four times as common as the table shows. The between-arm claims are untouched.

A second pair of passages cannot both be true of the cohort. Methods states BMI>30 and “we do not have a group of women with BMI below 30”; Table 2 prints BMI range 23.0–45.0. Mean 34.5 and median 34.0 still look like an obese sample, so a mistyped 23.0 for 33.0 remains live, but the two statements as printed conflict.

Table 1 copies “after lost follow up of 2 women” onto both arms. Interrupted analysed n=199 matches Methods and Figure 1 (one loss), not two. And Table 3’s subcutaneous-depth p=.127 does not come from a t-test on 4.5±1 vs 4.4±0.9 (that t-test is p=.296); both values are non-significant. Tests are never named, so a rank-sum remains possible; the other six Table 3 rows do match t-tests.

The numbers that support interrupted versus continuous closure reconcile with each other. The whole-cohort rates in the Results and Discussion, and the BMI inclusion statement, do not.

The arm-comparison figures check; the whole-cohort rates in the narrative and the body-mass-index range do not, and those contradictions need to be resolved before the descriptive results are used.

questions_for_authors.question: Results and Discussion state that wound gapping, seroma, erythema and infection occurred in 12%, 10%, 18% and 20% of the whole cohort, while Table 1 prints 12 (3), 10 (2.5), 18 (4.5) and 20 (5) of 397. Could you confirm which figures are the intended whole-cohort rates?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether the narrative rates are a count-as-percent transcription or a different analysis.

questions_for_authors.question: Methods states inclusion with BMI>30 and “we do not have a group of women with BMI below 30,” while Table 2 prints BMI range 23.0–45.0 (mean 34.5±3.6). Could you send the minimum BMI in the 397 analysed women?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether the 23.0 lower bound is a typo or an enrolment deviation from the stated criterion.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 3 reports subcutaneous tissue depth 4.5±1 vs 4.4±0.9, p=.127. An independent t-test on those means, SDs and n=198 vs 199 gives p≈.296. Could you say which test and software produced .127?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether the mismatch is an unnamed rank-sum (or other) procedure or a misreported p.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1’s Interrupted row reads “199 (50.1) after lost follow up of 2 women,” while Methods and Figure 1 give one interrupted loss and analysed n=199. Could you confirm the interrupted arm’s lost-to-follow-up count?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles a copied clause versus a real second loss that would make analysed n=198.

triage.reason: quote_not_located fired on all four accusations from PDF whitespace collapse; all four spans are in body.md verbatim, so the marker is global and the BMI finding is kept.
Pearson chi-square on [[10,188],[2,197]] reproduces p=.019 and Fisher OR=5.239; Wald p from the CI is a mixed SPSS pairing the paper never claimed.
Chi-square/Fisher from [[9,189],[1,198]] reproduces p=.011 and OR=9.429; the CI-implied Wald p is the same mixed-method pattern.
Pearson p=0.01538 from [[14,184],[4,195]] matches printed .015 and Fisher OR=3.709; not a p-versus-CI defect.
Absence of a named-test paragraph is a reporting gap, not arithmetic; it is named in limitations and in the depth-p assumptions.
